**Audience**: a tabular / CRM / fraud engineer who still sees XGBoost beat deep nets. **Empirical first**: leakage via sloppy target encoding; LightGBM blazing fast but biased on rare categories — then we name GBDT, GOSS, CatBoost, TabPFN.

Why tables resist deep learning: boosting math → tabular foundations.

### What you will be able to do

-   Justify with quantitative arguments the dominance of GBDTs on tabular data (small volumes, heterogeneous features, irregularities);
-   Derive boosting as gradient descent in a space of functions and connect approximation trees with shrinkage;
-   Compare the three engineering approaches — second-order regularization (XGBoost), histograms and leaf sampling (LightGBM), ordered encoding of categoricals (CatBoost) — and choose;
-   Encode categorical and numerical columns without information leakage;
-   Train deep tabular models (regularized MLPs, FT-Transformer) and know when they pay off;
-   Use TabPFN for in-context learning on a small table, and discuss its limits;
-   Serialize a table for an LLM, write and debug text-to-SQL queries;
-   Generate synthetic tabular data and build an honest benchmark, up to the final decision guide.

### Where this course fits in the program

M2 module offered in period 1, outside the recommended track, designed as an applied deepening accessible right after M1. **Prerequisites**: chapter 5 (trees, forests, boosting) of [Machine Learning](../m1p1-machine-learning/index.html) is the direct foundation — ch. 0 consolidates it before pushing the theory; the scikit-learn practice acquired in M1 suffices for the labs.

**Downstream modules**: data versioning, rigorous benchmarking, and computation costs of the [ML Ops and LLM Engineering Principles](../m2-mlops-llm-engineering/index.html) module naturally extend this course when tables become pipelines; and for your internships as for your first jobs, it is tabular data you will handle — this is the module you will use the soonest outside the School.

### Course outline

-   **Reminders: trees, forests, boosting** — reactivates CART trees, bagging, and random forests before shifting to a higher gear.
-   **Why GBDTs (still) dominate tabular data** — comparative studies and the structural reasons for superiority on tables.
-   **Boosting: functional gradient descent** — the complete mathematical re-derivation of what a library `fit` call hides.
-   **XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost: three engineering approaches** — what each library exactly optimizes, and at what price.
-   **Encoding columns: categorical and numerical** — target encoding, binning, and the leakage pitfalls that skew comparisons.
-   **Deep tabular: regularized MLPs and FT-Transformer** — what networks truly bring, and when they still lag behind.
-   **TabPFN: learning tables in-context** — a pre-trained transformer that classifies a table without gradients: how, why, up to where.
-   **LLMs and tables: serialization, text-to-SQL** — turning a database into text, querying in natural language, measuring error rates.
-   **Synthetic tabular data** — generating realistic tables for augmentation, testing, and sharing.
-   **Honest benchmarking** — protocols, fair search budgets, validation-set overfitting pitfalls.
-   **Choosing your method: guide and open questions** — the practitioner's practical decision tree, and what research has not settled yet.
-   **Exercises / Labs** — from hand-computed gradient boosting to the full comparative study on real data.
-   **References** — founding papers of GBDTs and tabular foundation models.

### How to study this module

-   Run the code as you read: each chapter comes with short experiments that must be reproduced to believe the curves.
-   Build your hyperparameter "reading grid" from ch. 2 onward: associate each parameter with its mathematical effect rather than its default value.
-   For GBDTs, read the `feature_importance` output with suspicion and train yourself to explain why it misleads; it is a job-interview reflex.
-   Redo the benchmark of ch. 9 on a dataset of your choice following the protocol: it is the most rewarding deliverable of the module.
-   Keep the final guide (ch. 10) at hand during the other modules and your internships: it is made to be used, not memorized.

::: note
[The LLGA perspective]{.tag} A master dedicated to LLMs and graphs might give the impression that tabular data is outdated; it is the opposite: it is the ground where foundation models have the most to prove, and where the industrial value of AI remains the most massive. By crossing the "statistics/trees" culture of data scientists with the "generative foundations" culture of LLGA, this module makes you able to choose the dominant tool in industry *and* to judge, without a manual, the next wave of tabular models.
:::

::: note
[Note Extrapolons]{.tag} Place in the 2-year path: concrete failure modes first, then names and theorems.
:::

## 0. Reminders: trees, forests, boosting {#ch0}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Reminders from the Machine Learning module (M1 P1, ch. 5) — what is assumed acquired
:::

-   **CART trees**: recursive partitions of the space by univariate thresholds $x_j \leq t$, splits chosen by maximizing the impurity decrease (Gini/variance), depth = control of the bias-variance trade-off;
-   **Bias-variance decomposition**: $\mathrm{Err} = \mathrm{bias}^2 + \mathrm{variance} + \mathrm{noise}$, and the role of *ensembles*: bagging and random forests reduce variance by averaging decorrelated trees;
-   **AdaBoost**: iterative reweighting of misclassified examples, prediction by weighted vote of weak classifiers;
-   **Gradient boosting**: at each iteration a small tree is fit *on the residuals* of the current model, then added with a step $\eta > 0$;
-   **Evaluation** (ch. 9): cross-validation, data leakage, benchmark protocols — we return to this in ch. 9 of the present module.
::::

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Notation of the module]{.tag} A **tabular dataset** is a matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ whose columns (features) are *heterogeneous*: numerical (price, age, log-ratio), categorical (country, product code), ordinal, binary, dates, sometimes textual; the target is $y \in \mathcal{Y}$ (classification) or $y \in \mathbb{R}$ (regression). We write $f$ for the model, $L$ for the loss, $\mathcal{D} = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ for the sample. A single row can contain scales ranging from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{7}$ and massively skewed columns — it is this heterogeneity that structures the whole module.
:::

::: note
[The module's storyline]{.tag} M1 (cf. Machine Learning module ch. 5) presented boosting as an idea: "one fits trees on the residuals". This module takes it seriously as a **central object of study**: (i) we prove the formulas of the industrial engines (optimal leaf weights, split gain, GOSS, ordered statistics); (ii) we explain *why* they win on tables, based on the large empirical studies of 2021-2025; (iii) we explore the two deep counter-attacks — attention over features (ch. 5) and tabular *foundations* (TabPFN, ch. 6) or linguistic ones (ch. 7); (iv) we finish with synthetic generation (ch. 8) and an honest comparison protocol (ch. 9), extending ch. 9 of the Machine Learning module.
:::

## 1. Why GBDTs (still) dominate tabular data {#ch1}

Concrete scene: a leaderboard win… with temporal leakage. This chapter sets why GBDTs still dominate.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} In-fold target encoding; ignoring trees' monotone invariance; comparing deep vs GBDT without a feature budget.
:::

Images, text, speech, and graphs have been conquered by deep networks. Tables — which remain the majority format of enterprise data (CRM, sensors, finance, health, logs) — resist. This finding was established rigorously by three major empirical studies, which serve as the module's guiding thread.

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — GBDT (extended reminder)]{.tag} A **gradient boosted decision tree** is an additive model $$ F_M(x) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} \eta\, h_m(x), $$ where each $h_m$ is a shallow regression tree fit on the negative of the gradient of the loss with respect to the current prediction (ch. 2). The structural hyperparameters: number of trees $M$, learning rate $\eta$, maximum depth (≈ order of interaction), subsampling rate (rows/columns), leaf regularization.
:::

::: thm
[Study 1.2 — Grinsztajn, Oyallon & Varoquaux (NeurIPS 2022)]{.tag} "*Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on typical tabular data?*": over dozens of medium-sized OpenML datasets (up to $\sim\!10,000$ rows, regression and classification), tree-based models (XGBoost, scikit-learn GBDT) systematically beat deep tabular networks, even after reasonable tuning. The paper isolates two mechanistic causes:

-   networks are **sensitive to uninformative features**: removing as many as possible helps networks far more than trees, which naturally "isolate" useful columns (a tree can simply never split on a useless column);
-   networks struggle with **irregular target functions**: neither smooth nor monotone, with "steps" and local interactions — the natural terrain of threshold splits.

A **random rotation** experiment on the columns confirms the diagnosis: after rotation, trees degrade sharply (their axis-aligned splits lose their meaning) whereas networks — rotation-invariant by construction — fare better: the *axis-aligned* structure of real tables is information that trees exploit and MLPs ignore.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.3 — Trees are invariant under monotone transformation of columns]{.tag} Let $h$ be a tree and, for each column $j$, $g_j : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ a strictly increasing function. If $\tilde{x}_j = g_j(x_j)$, then the tree trained on the transformed data induces *the same partition* of the space (up to the thresholds) and makes the same predictions. In particular: log-transforming, whitening, or clipping a skewed column changes (almost) nothing for a GBDT.

::: proof
A split $x_j \leq t$ partitions the examples into $\{i : x_{ij} \leq t\}$ and its complement. Since $g_j$ is strictly increasing, $x_{ij} \leq t \iff g_j(x_{ij}) \leq g_j(t)$: every split on $x_j$ is a split on $\tilde{x}_j$, with the image threshold $g_j(t)$. By recursion over the depth, the partitions coincide, so the leaves receive the same examples and the predictions (leaf means/majorities) are identical. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Why this proposition matters]{.tag} It explains a robust empirical result: GBDTs win especially when features have *skewed, heavy, multimodal* distributions — precisely the cases where a network, which adds and multiplies activations, suffers from scales and distribution tails, whereas a tree only looks at the order of values. McElfresh et al. (TabZilla, NeurIPS 2023: *When do neural nets outperform boosted trees on tabular data?*) quantifies this over 176 datasets and 19 algorithms: GBDTs dominate on skewed/heavy-tailed features, and the most decisive performance factor is not the model family but the **tuning budget** — "lightly tuning a GBDT matters more than choosing between a GBDT and a network".
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.4 — The 2021-2023 debate in three studies]{.tag} (i) Shwartz-Ziv & Armon (*Tabular data: Deep learning is not all you need*, Information Fusion 2022): XGBoost beats deep models on most of their datasets, and tuning does not close the gap; GBDT+network ensembles = the best of both. (ii) Grinsztajn et al. (2022): the gap is real at medium sizes and stems from inductive biases (study 1.2). (iii) McElfresh et al. (2023): on the largest available benchmark, no family dominates everywhere; a simple *hybrid* (average of a GBDT + a lightly tuned MLP) is the best "default". Moral: the question is not "which is best" but "in which regime" — the subject of ch. 10.
:::

## 2. Boosting: functional gradient descent {#ch2}

Boosting is most cleanly written as *gradient descent in the space of functions* — a view due to Friedman (2001), which generalizes AdaBoost (Freund & Schapire, 1997; cf. Machine Learning module ch. 5 for the historical account).

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Functional gradient descent]{.tag} We look for $F^\star = \arg\min_F \sum_i L(y_i, F(x_i))$ in a space of functions. The "gradient at point $x_i$" is the variable $r_i = -\left[\dfrac{\partial L(y_i, F(x_i))}{\partial F(x_i)}\right]_{F = F_{m-1}}$. The boosting iteration: (1) compute the $r_i$; (2) fit a weak learner $h_m$ (shallow tree) by least squares to the $r_i$; (3) update $F_m = F_{m-1} + \eta\, h_m$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — Residuals for the quadratic loss]{.tag} For $L(y, a) = \tfrac{1}{2}(y - a)^2$, one has exactly $r_i = y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i)$: "fitting on the residuals" is a special case of definition 2.1.

::: proof
$\partial L / \partial a = a - y$, so $-\partial L(y_i, F(x_i))/\partial F = y_i - F(x_i)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[The role of each ingredient]{.tag} **$\eta$ (shrinkage)**: a small step ⇒ each tree corrects what the previous ones left behind — equivalent to a regularization of the descent step, to be combined with more trees. **Subsampling** (Friedman, 2002): fitting each tree on a fraction of the rows injects bagging into the descent and decorrelates the trees (direct link with the M1 forests). **Limited depth**: a tree of depth $d$ models only order-$d$ interactions — boosting learns a sum of "simple piecewise" functions, which matches the irregularity of tabular targets (study 1.2). **Early stopping**: $M$ chosen on validation — the analogue of truncating an expansion.
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.3 — One iteration by hand]{.tag} Regression, quadratic loss, current model $F_0 \equiv \bar{y}$. Residuals $r_i = y_i - \bar{y}$. A depth-1 tree fit to the residuals chooses the column $j^\star$ and the threshold $t^\star$ minimizing the within-leaf variance of the $r_i$ — that is, best explaining *what the constant model could not say*. New prediction $F_1(x) = \bar{y} + \eta\,(a\, \mathbf{1}[x_{j^\star} \leq t^\star] + b\,\mathbf{1}[x_{j^\star} > t^\star])$, where $a, b$ are the per-leaf residual means. The following iterations attack the residuals of $F_1$, and so on.
:::

::: note
[What ch. 3 adds]{.tag} Definition 2.1 says *what* to fit; XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost optimize *how*: closed-form leaf weights via a second-order Taylor expansion, histogram-based splits, large-gradient sampling, symmetric trees, ordered statistics for categoricals. All choices that take the GBDT from "nice idea" to industrial default on tables.
:::

## 3. XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost: three engineering approaches to gradient {#ch3}

### 3.1. XGBoost: the second derivative and explicit regularization

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — XGBoost's regularized objective]{.tag} At iteration $t$, with $g_i = \partial_{\hat{y}^{(t-1)}_i} L(y_i, \hat{y}^{(t-1)}_i)$ and $h_i = \partial^2_{\hat{y}^{(t-1)}_i} L(y_i, \hat{y}^{(t-1)}_i)$, one minimizes $$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[ g_i\, f_t(x_i) + \tfrac{1}{2} h_i\, f_t(x_i)^2 \Big] + \Omega(f_t), \qquad \Omega(f) = \gamma\, T + \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{T} w_j^2, $$ where $f_t$ is a tree with $T$ leaves of weights $w_1, \dots, w_T$. This is the second-order Taylor expansion of the loss, exact for the quadratic loss, very good for the log-loss.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.2 — Optimal weights and split gain (XGBoost)]{.tag} For a fixed tree, write $G_j = \sum_{i \in \text{leaf } j} g_i$ and $H_j = \sum_{i \in \text{leaf } j} h_i$. Then $$ w_j^\star = -\frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda}, \qquad \mathcal{L}^\star = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{T}\frac{G_j^2}{H_j + \lambda} + \gamma T, $$ and splitting a parent node $P$ into $L, R$ improves the objective by $$ \mathrm{Gain} = \frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{G_L^2}{H_L + \lambda} + \frac{G_R^2}{H_R + \lambda} - \frac{(G_L + G_R)^2}{H_L + H_R + \lambda}\right] - \gamma. $$

::: proof
The objective factorizes per leaf: $\sum_j [\,w_j G_j + \tfrac{1}{2} w_j^2 (H_j + \lambda)\,] + \gamma T$ (the $\lambda$ completes the square). Each term is a trinomial in $w_j$ with minimum $w_j^\star = -G_j/(H_j + \lambda)$, of value $-\tfrac{1}{2}G_j^2/(H_j + \lambda)$. Hence $\mathcal{L}^\star$. A split replaces leaf $P$ (sums $G_P = G_L + G_R$, $H_P = H_L + H_R$) with two leaves: the gain is $\mathcal{L}^\star_P - \mathcal{L}^\star_{\{L,R\}}$, i.e. the stated expression; one splits only if Gain > 0, i.e. beyond the "price" $\gamma$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[The other pieces of XGBoost]{.tag} **Weighted quantile sketch**: proposing split thresholds via quantiles weighted by the $h_i$ (points with high curvature count more), with an approximation guarantee. **Sparsity-aware**: each node learns a "default direction" for missing values. **Column/row sampling**: random-forest-style bagging applied to boosting. The whole made XGBoost (2016) the reference engine of tabular competitions from 2015 onward.
:::

### 3.2. LightGBM: histograms, GOSS, EFB

::: def
[Definition 3.3 — Histogram-based splits]{.tag} Each numerical feature is pre-discretized into $B$ bins (typically 255); the $(g_i, h_i)$ are accumulated per bin, and the candidate thresholds are the bin boundaries. Cost per feature: $O(n)$ to build the histogram, instead of $O(n \log n)$ for sorting; in memory, the child histogram is derived from the parent by subtraction. The approximation error is bounded by the bin width — imperceptible in practice.
:::

::: def
[Definition 3.4 — GOSS (Gradient-based One-Side Sampling)]{.tag} Examples with *small* gradients are well predicted; one keeps the $a \cdot n$ examples with the largest $\|g_i\|$ (set $A$), randomly samples $b \cdot n$ examples from the rest ($B'$), and amplifies their gradients by a factor $(1-a)/b$. The split gain is computed on this weighted selection.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.5 — GOSS (approximately) preserves the gain]{.tag} With the weights $\tilde{g}_i = \frac{1-a}{b}\, g_i$ on $B'$, the estimator $\tilde{G}_j = \sum_{i \in A \cap j} g_i + \sum_{i \in B' \cap j} \tilde{g}_i$ is an (approximately) unbiased estimator of $G_j = \sum_{i \in j} g_i$, and likewise for the $H_j$ — hence the gain of theorem 3.2 is estimated consistently.

::: proof
Write $G_j = G_j^{A} + G_j^{\bar{A}}$. Uniform sampling of $B'$ in $\bar{A}$ gives $\mathbb{E}[\sum_{i \in B' \cap j} \tilde{g}_i] = \frac{1-a}{b}\, \mathbb{E}[\sum_{i \in B' \cap j} g_i] = \frac{1-a}{b} \cdot \frac{b}{1-a} G_j^{\bar{A}} = G_j^{\bar{A}}$, hence the expectation $G_j^{A} + G_j^{\bar{A}} = G_j$. The rest follows by replacing the sums with their estimators in the gain formula (second-order bias, negligible compared to the gain itself). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 3.6 — EFB (Exclusive Feature Bundling)]{.tag} In sparse data (massive one-hot), two columns are rarely nonzero simultaneously: they can share a "merged" bin. One builds a conflict graph (edge if frequent co-nonzero), greedily colors it to form groups of exclusive features; each bundle becomes a single histogram column. Combined with GOSS, this is the pair that gives LightGBM its speed gains.
:::

### 3.3. CatBoost: oblivious trees and ordered statistics

::: def
[Definition 3.7 — Oblivious trees]{.tag} An oblivious tree applies the *same* split to all nodes of a given level: depth $d$ gives exactly $d$ tests $(j_1, t_1), \dots, (j_d, t_d)$ and the result is indexed like an array of size $2^d$. Advantages: evaluation in $O(d)$, trivially vectorized execution, and strong regularization (higher bias, lower variance — the same logic as the limited depth of ch. 2).
:::

::: def
[Definition 3.8 — Ordered target statistics]{.tag} For a categorical $c$ and a random permutation $\sigma$ of the rows, the encoded value of row $i$ uses only *earlier* rows: $$ \hat{x}_i = \frac{\sum_{\sigma(k) < \sigma(i)} \mathbf{1}[c_k = c_i]\, y_k + a\, p}{\sum_{\sigma(k) < \sigma(i)} \mathbf{1}[c_k = c_i] + a}, $$ with $p$ a global prior (target mean) and $a$ a smoothing weight. This is target encoding (ch. 4) *without leakage*: row $i$ is never encoded with its own target. **Ordered boosting** generalizes the idea to residuals: each example is scored only by models that have not seen it — correcting the "prediction shift" of classical GBDTs (Prokhorenkova et al., 2018).
:::

                   XGBoost                                     LightGBM                                             CatBoost
  ---------------- ------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------
  Split            exact / approximate quantiles (2nd order)   histogram, leaf by leaf (leaf-wise)                  oblivious, level by level
  Acceleration     quantile sketch, sparsity-aware             GOSS + EFB (defs 3.4-3.6)                            symmetric trees, native GPU
  Categoricals     one-hot / provided encodings                partition of categories by gradient statistics       native ordered TS (def. 3.8)
  Inductive bias   regularization $\gamma, \lambda$          leaf-wise growth (beware overfitting on small $n$)   anti-leakage + symmetry

```python
# The same problem seen by the three engines (nearly identical APIs)
import xgboost as xgb, lightgbm as lgb, catboost as cb
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
Xtr, Xva, ytr, yva = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)

m1 = xgb.XGBClassifier(n_estimators=2000, learning_rate=0.02, max_depth=6,
                       early_stopping_rounds=100).fit(Xtr, ytr, eval_set=[(Xva, yva)])
m2 = lgb.LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=2000, learning_rate=0.02, num_leaves=63,
                        subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8).fit(
                        Xtr, ytr, eval_set=[(Xva, yva)],
                        callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(100)])
m3 = cb.CatBoostClassifier(iterations=2000, learning_rate=0.02, depth=8,
                           cat_features=cat_idx, early_stopping_rounds=100).fit(
                           Xtr, ytr, eval_set=(Xva, yva), verbose=False)
```

## 4. Encoding columns: categorical and numerical {#ch4}

On tables, a massive share of the performance is decided *before* the model: GBDTs barely digest massive one-hots, networks require clean numerical inputs. This chapter surveys the encodings, with the central pitfall: target leakage.

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Target encoding (mean encoding)]{.tag} For a high-cardinality categorical $c$ (postal codes, SKUs, users), one replaces the category with a statistic of the target; smoothed version of Micci-Barreca (2001): $$ \mathrm{enc}(v) = \frac{n_v\, \bar{y}_v + m\, \bar{y}}{n_v + m}, $$ where $\bar{y}_v$ is the target mean within category $v$, $n_v$ its count, $\bar{y}$ the global mean and $m$ a pseudo-count: rare categories are pulled toward the global prior.
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.2 — Leakage, demonstrated]{.tag} Suppose a column "identifier" unique per row ($n_v = 1$ everywhere) and a target *independent* of everything (pure noise). Naive target encoding (computed on the whole train set, row included) gives $\mathrm{enc}(v_i) = y_i$: the feature contains *exactly* the target. Any model reaches a training AUC of 1.0, while the test AUC falls back to 0.5. The model has learned nothing: it copies. With intermediate cardinality, the leakage is partial ($\mathrm{enc}(v)$ mixes $y_i$ and $\bar{y}_v$) — even more dangerous, because invisible on naive metrics.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 4.3 — Anti-leakage: out-of-fold and random order]{.tag} Two standard repairs: (i) **K-fold out-of-fold**: split the train set into $K$ blocks, encode each block with the statistics of the other $K-1$; (ii) **random order** (CatBoost, def. 3.8): each row encoded using only earlier rows. In both cases, $\mathrm{enc}(v_i)$ becomes independent of $y_i$ conditionally on the category — the leakage disappears at the cost of a slight estimation noise, absorbed by the smoothing $m$.
:::

::: def
[Definition 4.4 — One-hot vs embeddings]{.tag} **One-hot**: $K$ binary columns: no similarity assumption between categories, but dimension $K$ (disastrous for large $K$, and cf. EFB). **Entity embeddings** (Guo & Berkhahn, 2016): each category $v$ receives a learned vector $z_v \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ ($d \ll K$), via a table embedded in the network: categories that behave similarly with respect to the target move closer — the embeddings of "Bavaria" and "Baden-Württemberg" (Rossmann competition) end up neighbors. This is the natural bridge between categoricals and networks; GBDTs, for their part, prefer native target encoding or splits by category partitions.
:::

::: def
[Definition 4.5 — Numerical feature embeddings]{.tag} Three families to "textualize" a scalar in the eyes of a network (Gorishniy et al., NeurIPS 2022):

-   **Linear**: $e_j = b_j + x_j w_j$ (the FT-Transformer tokenizer, ch. 5);
-   **Periodic**: $e_j = [\sin(2\pi c_j x_j), \cos(2\pi c_j x_j)]_{c_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)}$, parameters $\sigma$ (or the $c_j$) learned — a kernel-type building block;
-   **Piecewise (piecewise-linear binning)**: $x_j \to$ interpolation coordinates over $B$ bins defined by quantiles — a controlled return to the "histogram logic" of GBDTs.

Massive empirical result: a simple MLP with good numerical embeddings rivals sophisticated architectures.
:::

::: note
[Engineering, not magic]{.tag} Networks inherit the M1 reflexes: standardize *per column* (never globally), transform heavy distributions (rank/quantile), extract dates (day of week, holidays, $\sin/\cos$ cyclicity of the hour), cross business columns (income/spending), and handle missing values by imputation + indicator (networks have no XGBoost-style default direction — GBDTs do; cf. ch. 3). Proposition 1.3 reminds us why all this only benefits networks: trees do not care.
:::

  Encoding                Good cardinality   Leakage?            GBDT                                  Networks
  ----------------------- ------------------ ------------------- ------------------------------------- ---------------------------
  One-hot                 low                no                  mediocre (sparse)                     well (dense layer)
  Ordinal                 —                  no                  native CatBoost/LightGBM compatible   false ordering — to avoid
  Naive target encoding   high               **yes** (ex. 4.2)   trap                                  trap
  OOF / ordered target    high               no                  excellent                             well
  Entity embeddings       high               no (learned)        via pre-training                      excellent (def. 4.4)

## 5. Deep tabular: regularized MLPs and FT-Transformer {#ch5}

Two deep answers to the dominance of trees: better regularize MLPs, and treat the *columns* as tokens of a transformer — attention playing the role of a differentiable interaction engine.

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Feature tokenizer (FT-Transformer)]{.tag} Each column becomes a token of dimension $d$: for a numerical one, $e_j = b_j + x_j\, w_j$ ($b_j, w_j \in \mathbb{R}^d$ learned); for a categorical one, a row of an embedding table. To this one adds a $[\mathrm{CLS}]$ token. The following block is a standard transformer (multi-head attention, cf. Deep Learning module): $$ \mathrm{Att}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V, $$ computed *between features* of the same row. The prediction is read from $[\mathrm{CLS}]$ after $L$ blocks.
:::

::: note
[Why feature-wise attention changes things]{.tag} An MLP must *sample* interactions via its weights; a tree builds them greedily; the transformer learns, for each pair of columns, a conditional interaction weight (the heads saturate on useful pairs and "switch off" useless columns — a partial answer to the sensitivity to uninformative features of study 1.2). Gorishniy et al. (NeurIPS 2021) show that the FT-Transformer is the most consistent tabular network, at an equal tuning budget — and that the tokenizer/def. 4.5 accounts for much of it.
:::

::: ex
[Example 5.2 — Two other families]{.tag} **TabNet** (Arik & Pfister, AAAI 2021): *per-instance* selection of a small group of features (sparse masks learned via a sparsemax) at each step — a differentiable echo of the trees' "column selection", with the masks offered as interpretability. **NODE** (Popov et al., 2020): *differentiable* oblivious trees (entmax splits over thresholds) trained end-to-end — boosting rewritten as a network. **Regularized MLPs** (Kadra et al., 2021): a well-tuned "cocktail" of regularizations suffices to hold the comparison — confirming that on tables, the essence of the game is played on inductive biases and tuning.
:::

::: thm
[Peculiarities of tables (summary)]{.tag}

-   **Heterogeneous columns**: mixed types, scales, semantics — no "natural" convolution kernel;
-   **No translation invariance** nor locality: permuting *pixels* changes nothing in an image, permuting *columns* changes everything; the rotation experiment of ch. 1 shows that this absence of invariance is a richness (axis-aligned structure) that MLPs do not exploit;
-   **Irregular distributions**: skewness, heavy tails, multimodality, "round" regulatory thresholds;
-   **Many uninformative features** and **informative missing values**;
-   **Small/medium $n$** by vision standards: the risk of overfitting the architecture is real (cf. TabZilla, ch. 9).
:::

## 6. TabPFN: learning tables in-context {#ch6}

The 2023-2025 paradigm shift: no longer train a model *on* the table, but train a transformer *once and for all* on millions of synthetic tables, then predict *in-context* — the tabular analogue of LLM few-shot learning.

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Prior-fitted network (PFN)]{.tag} Let a **prior** $\mathfrak{p}$ over datasets: a law over functions $f$ (and noises, features, sizes) from which synthetic datasets $\mathcal{D}_{sim}$ are drawn. A PFN is a transformer $q_\theta$ trained to predict, for an example $x$ presented next to a set $\mathcal{D}_{train}$ *inside its input window*, the law $p(y \mid x, \mathcal{D}_{train})$. Müller et al. (ICLR 2022) show that such a network approximates the **Bayesian posterior predictive** $$ p(y \mid x, \mathcal{D}) = \int p(y \mid x, \theta)\, p(\theta \mid \mathcal{D})\, d\theta $$ in *a single forward pass*: the transformer's in-context learning is a form of amortized Bayesian inference. Cf. LLMs module (M2) ch. 3 for in-context learning on the language side.
:::

::: def
[Definition 6.2 — TabPFN's causal prior]{.tag} TabPFN (Hollmann et al., ICLR 2023; v2: Nature 2025) draws its synthetic tables from random **structural causal models**: random DAG over $p$ variables, nonlinear mechanisms (networks, piecewise transformations), heterogeneous noises, then monotone marginal transformations — mimicking the "irregular distributions" of ch. 5 — and adding uninformative features and missing values. By training on millions of such tables, the model learns *to learn:* in use, one deposits train + the row to predict in the context; no gradient descent is run on the user's table.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 6.3 — What in-context buys]{.tag} (i) **Zero pipeline hyperparameters** (no trees, rates, or depths): the "tuning" is amortized in pre-training; (ii) **seconds** of inference for tables up to $\sim\!10,000$ rows (v2), classification *and* regression, missing values and outliers tolerated; (iii) **free uncertainty**: $q_\theta(y \mid x, \mathcal{D})$ is a predictive law — usable for abstention. Trade-offs: a context window (beyond $\sim\!10,000$ rows, fall back to "classical" training minibatches), limited types (no rich textual columns; cf. ch. 7), and a dependence on the proximity between the real table and the prior of def. 6.2.
:::

::: ex
[Example 6.4 — A shifting benchmark]{.tag} On the reference suites of medium-sized datasets, v2 (Nature 2025) beats tuned GBDTs on average — the first credible "deep" victory in this regime, three years after Grinsztajn et al. Ch. 9 nonetheless requires reading these results with a symmetric protocol (GBDT tuning budget, same folds, same seeds): the "trees vs foundations" debate remains open for large $n$, textual columns, and industrial constraints.
:::

## 7. LLMs and tables: serialization, text-to-SQL {#ch7}

An LLM does not read a table: it reads text. Everything goes through a **serialization** — and this engineering choice is as decisive as the prompt itself.

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Usual serializations of a row]{.tag} For a row $(x_1, \dots, x_p)$ with named columns $c_1, \dots, c_p$: CSV aligned on a header; JSON key-value; Markdown; textual template ("*The patient is $x_{age}$ years old, receives $x_{dose}$ mg…*"); the "schema" (column names, types, description) can precede the series. Two critical properties: the **column order** influences the prediction (the model is sensitive to token positions), and the **column names** activate pre-training knowledge ("country", "dosage") — a semantic prior that no GBDT has.
:::

::: thm
[Study 7.2 — TabLLM (Hegselmann et al., 2023)]{.tag} In **few-shot** (typically $\leq 64$ examples), an LLM (T0/GPT-3.5, textual serializations) predicts tables better than dedicated deep methods and rivals GBDTs; the advantage reverses as soon as data abounds — the per-row token cost becomes prohibitive and the semantic prior no longer compensates for the statistical capacity. The LLM wins where *every example is expensive* (medical annotation, industry); the GBDT where data is massive.
:::

::: def
[Definition 7.3 — Text-to-SQL and schema linking]{.tag} When the table is a database, the LLM becomes an *interface*: producing SQL from a question in natural language. **Schema linking** denotes the step of aligning question ↔ schema: entities of the question to cells of the tables, terms to candidate columns/tables, then plausible joins. Benchmarks: **Spider** (Yu et al., 2018; clean schemas, academic questions) then **BIRD** (Li et al., 2023; 95 large "dirty" databases, dirty values, external knowledge, query efficiency requirement) — on which the performance drop of models between the two worlds is precisely measured.
:::

```python
# Three postures of the LLM facing a table
# 1) Predict: serialized row -> label (TabLLM, few-shot)
prompt = f"Column 'dosage_mg': {x['dose']}; 'age': {x['age']}; ...\nAnswer (0/1)?"
# 2) Engineer: propose features / clean / document the columns
#    (the LLM writes the feature engineering code, the GBDT predicts)
# 3) Query: natural language question -> SQL (schema linking + BIRD)
question = "top 5 clients by margin in 2025, excluding refunds"
# -> SELECT c.id, SUM(o.marge) FROM ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT 5;
```

::: note
[Structural limits]{.tag} Tokenization of numbers (scalars are chopped into pieces — fine arithmetic remains fragile); context window (millions of rows will never fit); confidentiality (sending customer rows to an API; cf. the Explainability, Security and Privacy of LLMs module); cost and non-determinism in production (cf. ML Ops module). Hence the dominant posture: **hybrid** — the LLM prepares, summarizes, links, programs; the tabular model (GBDT/TabPFN) predicts.
:::

## 8. Synthetic tabular data {#ch8}

::: def
[Definition 8.1 — The fidelity-utility-privacy triangle]{.tag} A tabular generator $\mathcal{D}_{syn} \sim G(\mathcal{D}_{real})$ is judged on three axes in tension: **fidelity** (marginals and dependencies reproduced; KS/TV distances per column, correlations, detectability by a real-vs-synthetic classifier), **utility** (does a model trained on the synthetic perform on the real? the *train-synthetic-test-real* protocol, TSTR), and **privacy** (no synthetic row should copy an individual; nearest-neighbor distance metrics and membership inference attacks — cf. ch. 8 of the Security and Robustness module).
:::

::: ex
[Example 8.2 — Three families of generators]{.tag} **GAN/VAE**: CTGAN/TVAE (Xu et al., 2019) — "mode-based" normalization of multimodal columns (GMM) and a conditional classifier for categoricals. **Diffusion**: TabDDPM (Kotelnikov et al., ICML 2023) — Gaussian diffusion for numericals, multinomial diffusion for categoricals (cf. Image Synthesis module for the diffusion foundation), with missing-value imputation as a bonus. **Language models**: GReaT (Borisov et al., ICLR 2023) — one fine-tunes an LM on rows serialized as text with *random column order*; generating = sampling conditioned completions — the most faithful on dependencies, the most exposed to memorization (cf. LLMs module for LM memorization).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 8.3 — Synthetic ≠ anonymous]{.tag} A generator trained by maximum likelihood *memorizes*: rare rows (atypical individuals) can be reproduced almost verbatim. The formal safeguard is **differential privacy** (cf. Emerging ML module ch. 5): training the generator in DP (Gaussian mechanism on gradients) guarantees an $(\varepsilon, \delta)$ — at the price of a measurable fidelity loss. In practice one combines: DP when the guarantee is required, membership inference audits and nearest-record distances otherwise, and documentation of both (regulation; cf. ML Ops module).
:::

::: note
[Secondary uses]{.tag} Data augmentation to rebalance rare classes, pipeline testing ("twin datasets" for ML regression tests), cross-entity sharing (banks/suppliers without exchanging real rows), and — back to ch. 6 — synthetic generation is *also* the training technology of PFNs: TabPFN's prior is nothing other than a controlled causal table generator. The loop is closed between "learning from synthetic" and "generating synthetic".
:::

## 9. Honest benchmarking {#ch9}

The "trees vs deep vs foundations" debate has produced more contradictory conclusions than any other area of ML — almost always because of asymmetric protocols. This chapter sets the method required in all the module's labs (an extension of ch. 9 of the Machine Learning module).

::: thm
[Protocol rules]{.tag}

1.  **Same folds, same preprocessing** for everyone: seeded splits, encodings computed only inside the CV loop (the OOF target encoding of prop. 4.3 is *inside* the CV, never before);
2.  **Symmetric tuning budget**: same number of trials, same search, same selection metric — TabZilla shows that the tuning budget dominates the family choice (ch. 1);
3.  **Multiple seeds** (≥ 5) and report mean ± standard deviation: on medium tables, the inter-seed std of a GBDT can approach the gap between families;
4.  **Counted cost**: training + inference + tuning time (TabPFN's "zero-tuning" is compared to a *tuned* XGBoost — but also to default XGBoost);
5.  **Dataset deduplication**: OpenML suites share variants of the same dataset — a "win by average" benchmark may count the same dataset three times;
6.  **Test reuse**: forbidden — a test set that served to select a family no longer measures anything (benchmark overfitting).
:::

::: ex
[Example 9.1 — Calibrating an "X% better"]{.tag} On 20 OpenML datasets: mean GBDT AUC 0.812 ± 0.004 (5 seeds), FT-Transformer 0.807 ± 0.006, TabPFN 0.818 ± 0.000 (deterministic). Before writing "TabPFN wins": (i) paired per-dataset test (permutation or corrected t); (ii) check that the GBDT had its budget; (iii) look at the distribution — gaining 0.006 everywhere is not gaining 0.06 on half the datasets and losing on the other half; (iv) report the total time to prediction. The honest conclusion is often "statistically tied, choose by cost and constraint" (ch. 10).
:::

## 10. Choosing your method: guide and open questions {#ch10}

  Regime                                                                         Recommended default                             Why
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ ----------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------------------------------------
  $n \lesssim 10,000$, no tuning resources                                      TabPFN                                          zero hyperparameters, seconds, uncertainty included (prop. 6.3)
  Heterogeneous, skewed tables, medium/large $n$                                 GBDT (XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost)                monotone invariance (prop. 1.3), irregularity (study 1.2), cost
  Very large $n$, multimodal columns (linked text/image), differentiable stack   Tabular network (FT-Transformer) + embeddings   shared representations, joint gradients (ch. 5)
  Few-shot with semantic columns, free text                                      LLM (prediction or feature engineering)         pre-training prior (study 7.2)
  Anonymization / sharing / rebalancing                                          Synthetic generator + audit                     triangle of def. 8.1

::: note
[Open questions 2026]{.tag} (i) **Scaling of tabular foundations**: does pre-training on synthetic priors follow exploitable scaling laws, and how far can one go in $n$/$p$? (ii) **Transfer across schemas**: can a model trained "cold" on millions of tables specialize in-context to a *new* business schema? (iii) **Theory of tabular in-context**: what does the PFN exactly compute — a true Bayesian average, a kernel regression, something else? (iv) **Benchmarks**: deduplicated suites, counted cost, industrial constraints (drift, structured missing values); cf. ch. 9. These questions feed the master's internship/lab topics.
:::

## Exercises / Labs {#ex}

1.  **Theorem 3.2 by hand (ch. 2-3).** Implement in pure NumPy (without a library) a depth-1 tree boosting: residuals, leaf weights $w_j^\star = -G_j/(H_j+\lambda)$, split gain — verify on a toy dataset that the objective of theorem 3.2 decreases by exactly the announced Gain at each split.
2.  **GOSS and EFB (ch. 3).** In a toy GBDT: implement GOSS ($a = 0.2, b = 0.1$) and numerically verify proposition 3.5 (compare estimated gains with exact gains over 100 splits); build a sparse one-hot and measure the achievable EFB fusion rate (greedy coloring of the conflict graph).
3.  **Target encoding leakage (ch. 4 — central lab).** On a dataset where the target is pure noise: (i) naive target encoding with an identifier column — measure train/test AUC; (ii) intermediate cardinality (100 categories) — show that partial leakage skews standard CV; (iii) repair with K-fold OOF and Micci-Barreca smoothing (sweep $m$); (iv) rerun CatBoost with native ordered TS and compare.
4.  **Symmetric benchmark (ch. 5-6-9).** On 8-10 OpenML datasets (Grinsztajn suite): XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost with an equal tuning budget (Optuna, 100 trials), FT-Transformer (tokenizer + periodic embeddings), TabPFN. Same folds, 5 seeds, mean ± standard deviation, paired test, total time reported — write the "TabZilla-style" conclusion (ch. 9) then the decision guide (ch. 10) on these data.
5.  **Prior and in-context (ch. 6).** Generate tables from random SCMs (def. 6.2 — DAG skeleton, piecewise mechanisms, marginal transformations); train a small PFN transformer to predict $p(y\|x, \mathcal{D})$; show in-context learning (performance curve vs context size) and test sensitivity to the prior (Gaussian vs causal prior — when does the PFN fail?).
6.  **LLM on a table (ch. 7).** Serialize a tabular dataset in 4 formats (CSV/JSON/Markdown/template): measure the effect of format and column order in few-shot (16/64 examples); compare with a GBDT at the same sample sizes — reproduce the crossover of study 7.2; finish with 5 text-to-SQL questions on a mini-database and audit the schema linking errors.
7.  **Synthetic and privacy (ch. 8).** Generate data with CTGAN, TabDDPM, and a serialized LM (GReaT-like); evaluate fidelity (KS, correlations, detectability) and utility (TSTR vs TRTR); launch a membership inference attack and a nearest-record-distance analysis; redo the generator with light DP and plot the fidelity-privacy curve.
8.  **Rotation and useless features (ch. 1).** Reproduce the two diagnostics of Grinsztajn et al. on 3 datasets: (i) random column rotation — GBDT vs MLP; (ii) adding noise features then importance-based pruning — who suffers most? Reread proposition 1.3 in light of the results.
